c.tagline: Where East meets West amid minarets, cafes and mountains.

taxi.fareNote: Flag fall around 2.5 KM plus roughly 1 KM per km; always confirm the meter is running or agree a price beforehand.

emergency.note: Fire brigade: 123. General EU-style emergency 112 also works.

avoid.reason: Very safe in town; uncleared landmines remain in some rural areas — stay on marked paths/roads

hood_desc: The historic Ottoman-era old town of cobblestone lanes, copper workshops, mosques and cafes; best for first-time visitors who want to be steps from every major sight and nightlife.
The modern civic and business heart with government buildings, the Holiday Hotel, shopping and the National Museum; suits business travelers and those wanting easy tram access.
The main pedestrian shopping street (Ferhadija) linking old and new town, lined with cafes, boutiques and Austro-Hungarian architecture; good for travelers who want a central, walkable base.
A steep, atmospheric hillside quarter inside the old city walls with the Yellow Fortress and sweeping views; suits travelers wanting a quiet, authentic residential feel with fewer crowds.
A leafy spa town at the city's edge near the airport and Vrelo Bosne park; suits those seeking a relaxed, green base with thermal spas, away from the downtown bustle.
lodging: Hotel Hills Sarajevo Congress & Thermal Spa Resort

water.note: Fed by mountain springs and considered safe, though many visitors opt for bottled water as extra precaution.

transit.pay: Buy paper tickets from kiosks (cheaper) or pay the driver in cash for a slightly higher fare; validate tickets on board. A rechargeable BUS PLUS card is also available for frequent riders.
transit.hours: Trams and buses run roughly 05:00-23:00; limited night bus coverage after that, so taxis are the main late-night option.
transit.note: The Sarajevo tram, running since 1885, is one of the oldest urban tram systems in Europe.

train: Sarajevo Main Railway Station (services to Zagreb, Budapest via Mostar/Ploče lines vary)

tip.r: Rounding up the bill or leaving 10% at restaurants is appreciated but not obligatory.

food.name: Cevapi
food.desc: Small skinless beef sausages grilled over charcoal and packed into a warm somun flatbread with raw onion and kajmak.

places.name: Cevabdzinica Zeljo

places.name: Cevabdzinica Mrkva
places.note: Busy modern grill on the main cevapi street with consistently good somun.

places.name: Petica Ferhatovic
places.note: Long-running family grill, a favourite for slightly coarser, meatier cevapi.

food.name: Burek and Bosnian pita
food.desc: Hand-rolled filo coiled with minced beef (burek proper) or cheese, spinach or potato, baked under a metal sac lid.

places.name: Buregdzinica Bosna
places.note: Old-town standby turning out coils of burek all day; sold by weight.

places.name: Buregdzinica Sac
places.note: Bakes under the traditional sac lid, giving a crisper, smokier crust.

places.name: ASDZ Ascinica
places.note: Canteen-style spot serving pita alongside home-style stews.

food.name: Begova corba
food.desc: Bey's soup: a thick, creamy broth of chicken, okra and root vegetables finished with sour cream, dating to Ottoman Sarajevo.

places.name: ASDZ Ascinica
places.note: Classic point-and-pick ascinica; the go-to cheap lunch for begova corba and bread.

places.name: Inat Kuca
places.note: The 'Spite House' opposite City Hall, serving old Bosnian dishes since the 1990s.

places.name: Kibe Mahala
places.note: Hillside restaurant with city views and a strongly traditional Bosnian menu.

food.name: Bosanski lonac
food.desc: Bosnian pot: layers of beef, cabbage, potato, carrot and peppers sealed in an earthenware crock and baked for hours.

places.name: Kibe Mahala
places.note: Wood-fired kitchen best known for spit-roast lamb and slow-cooked pot dishes.

places.name: Inat Kuca
places.note: Tourist-friendly but genuinely traditional roster of Bosnian classics.

places.name: Dveri
places.note: Tiny, cluttered old-town room doing homely cooking and Bosnian wines.

food.name: Japrak and dolma
food.desc: Vine or chard leaves and hollowed peppers and onions stuffed with rice and minced meat, stewed until soft and served with yoghurt.

places.name: ASDZ Ascinica
places.note: Trays of stuffed vegetables change daily; point at what looks best.

places.name: Kibe Mahala
places.note: Refined versions of the home-style stuffed dishes with a view over the valley.

places.name: Dveri
places.note: Small kitchen with sogan-dolma and japrak among the daily specials.

food.name: Tufahija
food.desc: A whole apple poached in sugar syrup, cored and stuffed with sweetened walnuts, topped with cream and served in its own syrup.

places.name: Slasticarna Ramis
places.note: Old-town sweet shop that is the classic stop for tufahija and baklava.

places.name: Slasticarna Egipat
places.note: Long-established patisserie on the main pedestrian street.

places.name: Slasticarna Badem
places.note: Small traditional sweets counter beside the coppersmiths' lane.

food.name: Bosanska kafa
food.desc: Finely ground coffee boiled in a copper dzezva and served with a sugar cube and rahat lokum; a slow ritual, not a quick shot.

places.name: Ministry of Cejf
places.note: Specialty roaster that also serves properly made traditional Bosnian coffee.

places.name: Caffe Divan
places.note: Courtyard cafe inside the restored Ottoman caravanserai Moricia Han.

places.name: Zlatna Ribica
places.note: Eccentric antique-filled bar near the eternal flame; coffee and rakija both.

food.name: Sarajevsko pivo
food.desc: Beer brewed at the Sarajevska Pivara since 1864, whose spring kept parts of the city in water during the siege.

places.name: Pivnica HS
places.note: Grand beer hall attached to the brewery itself, with tank-fresh Sarajevsko.

places.name: Zlatna Ribica
places.note: Characterful late-night bar for beer and homemade rakija.

places.name: Bravadziluk bars

landmarks: Latin Bridge
This unassuming Ottoman-era stone bridge is world-famous as the site of Archduke Franz Ferdinand's 1914 assassination, the spark that ignited World War I.
Baščaršija
Sarajevo's historic Ottoman bazaar bursts with copper workshops, cafes serving Bosnian coffee, and cobblestone lanes that make it the city's most beloved quarter.
Sebilj Fountain
This ornate wooden Ottoman fountain in the middle of Baščaršija square is Sarajevo's most photographed symbol, surrounded by flocks of pigeons and cafe tables.
Gazi Husrev-beg Mosque
The largest and most important Ottoman mosque in the Balkans, this 16th-century masterpiece anchors Sarajevo's old town with its elegant dome and minaret.
City Hall (Vijećnica)
This flamboyant Moorish Revival building, rebuilt after wartime destruction, houses the National Library and remains Sarajevo's most striking piece of Austro-Hungarian architecture.
Tunnel of Hope Museum
This preserved wartime tunnel, dug beneath the airport during the 1990s siege, offers a sobering, powerful look at how Sarajevo survived years of blockade.
Sacred Heart Cathedral
Sarajevo's largest Catholic cathedral, with its twin neo-Gothic spires, anchors the city center and symbolizes Bosnia's multi-religious character alongside nearby mosques and churches.
Old Orthodox Church
One of the oldest Serbian Orthodox churches in Bosnia, this modest but historic sanctuary holds a treasury of centuries-old icons and manuscripts.
Trebević Cable Car
Rebuilt after wartime destruction, this cable car whisks visitors above the city to Trebević mountain, delivering sweeping panoramic views of Sarajevo below.
Ferhadija Street (Meeting of Cultures)
This pedestrian street marks the literal line where Ottoman East meets Austro-Hungarian West, a unique and walkable symbol of Sarajevo's crossroads identity.

train.note: The scenic Sarajevo-Mostar-Ploce train to the Croatian coast is seasonal, running on summer weekends only (returned for summer 2026) - it is the country's only international train. Domestic trains from Sarajevo station serve Mostar/Capljina and Zenica-Banja Luka.

intl.to: Zagreb, Split, Dubrovnik, Vienna, Germany & beyond

bus.note: Most departures use the main bus station next to the railway station. Buses to Serbia and some Montenegro routes leave instead from the East Sarajevo (Istocno Sarajevo) bus station across town - double-check which one your ticket uses.

ferry.note: Bosnia and Herzegovina has no ferry ports (its short coast at Neum has no passenger service). The nearest international and island ferries sail from Split and Dubrovnik in Croatia, both reachable by bus.

half.name: Tuzla
half.blurb: Bosnian city known for its salt-mining history and unique salt lake in the city center.

full.name: Podgorica

full.name: Banja Luka
full.blurb: Riverside city on the Vrbas known for its cathedral, parks, and relaxed Balkan café culture.

full.name: Novi Sad
